Stiff-man syndrome is a rare neurological disorder characterized by skeletal muscle rigidity and spasms in which 
detection of circulating anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies has suggested an autoimmune pathogenesis. TO 
further define the role of autoimmunity in the pathogenesis, we studied anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies, 
as well as organ- and non-organ-specific autoantibodies in 13 patients with stiff-man syndrome and 127 patients with 
other neurological disorders. Thyrogastric antibodies were more frequent in patients with stiff-man syndrome (46%) 
than in those with other neurological disorders (12%) (p < 0.05). Non-organ-specific antibodies were found at a 
similar frequency in the patients with stiff-man syndrome (61%) and those with other neurological disorders (65%). 
Islet-cell autoantibodies and anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies were more common in stiff-man syndrome 
patients (38% and 31%) compared to the patients with other neurological disorders (6% and 396, respectively; fi < 
0.001). With the exception of 1 patient in the other neurological disorders group, anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase 
antibodies were always associated with islet-cell autoantibodies. Four patients with stiff-man syndrome had an associ- 
ated solid tumor: 3 of them had antibodies recognizing a 125/130-kd protein and not glutamic acid decarboxylase. 
Our study indicates that with immunological markers, patients with stiff-man syndrome can be subdivided into 
three groups: (1) patients with circulating islet-cell autoantibodies, anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase as well as other 
organ-specific autoantibodies, and the frequent association with an autoimmune disease (autoimmune variant); (2) 
patients with associated neoplasms and circulating non-organ-specific autoantibodies but neither islet-cell nor anti- 
glutamic acid decarboxylase autoantibodies (paraneoplastic variant); and (3) patients with no evidence of any known 
autoantibody or association with other clinically evident diseases (idiopathic variant). We conclude that the presence of 
anti-glutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies is restricted to a subgroup of stiff-man syndrome patients with associated 
autoimmune diseases. The absence of these antibodies does not exclude a diagnosis of stiff-man syndrome, which is 
still based on clinical and neurophysiological evidence.

Stiff-man syndrome (SMS), a rare neurological disor- 
der first described by Moersch and Woltman in 1956 
111, is characterized by painful persistent axial and 
proximal limb muscle rigidity, which is aggravated by 
sensory stimuli and abolished by sleep and anesthesia 
El]. Electromyography of affected muscles at rest 
shows spontaneous constant firing of normal motor 
units in a full recruitment pattern, reinforced by pas- 
sive and voluntary movements {2]. The muscle con- 
traction tends to become chronic and leads the patient 
to a state of constant rigidity that is only relieved 
by systemic administration of benzodiazepines or other 
y-aminobutyric acid (GABA) ag-onists 12-41,

The etiopathogenesis of SMS is still obscure. Recent 
studies [S, 61 demonstrated circulating autoantibodies 
directed against the GABAergic nerve terminals in up 
to 60% of SMS patients, and suggested an autoim- 
mune-mediated impairment of GABAergic neuro- 
transmission due to autoreactivity to the GABA- 
converting enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase 
(GAD). However, anti-GAD antibodies are not exclu- 
sive of SMS patients: They have been reported in the 
majority of patients with insulin-dependent diabetes 
mellitus (IDDM) without any sign or symptom of mus- 
cle rigidity {7}, and in at least 1 patient with IDDM 
and another neurological disorder unrelated to SMS 
[S). Moreover, the existence of a group of anti-GAD 
antibody-negative, otherwise typical SMS patients r9- 
1 11 further questions the pathogenetic relevance of 
these antibodies in SMS.

Patient Selection 
We collected serum samples from 13 patients (5 males and 
8 females; mean age, 48 years) with a diagnosis of SMS (mean 
disease duration, 4 years) according to accepted criteria 
11-31, Two of the SMS patients also had IDDM; 1 of them 
had Graves' disease; and 4 of them had an associated neo- 
plasm, including colon adenocarcinoma, breast adenocarci- 
noma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, and thymorna. The latter pa- 
tient had also myasthenia gravis [lo]. The remaining ? 
patients with SMS had no clinical evidence of other associ- 
ated diseases. Seven of the 13 SMS patients have been previ- 
ously described C5, 6, 9-12}. Oligoclonal bands were found 
in only two of the eight cerebrospinal fluid samples from 
SMS patients studied c5, 91. 
Serum samples were also collected from 127 patients with 
other neurological disorders including multiple sclerosis (j7),

Discussion 
The finding of anti-GAD antibodies in a proportion of 
SMS patients has suggested an autoimmune-mediated 
pathogenesis of this rare disorder {5, 6). Accordingly, 
an autoantibody-mediated attack against GABAergic 
transmission may impair the cerebellar control of mus- 
cle tone. However, the presence of circulating anti- 
GAD antibodies in a large proportion of IDDM pa-

tients without clinical or electrophysiological signs of 
motor-unit hyperactivity [7) questions the relevance of 
anti-GAD antibodies in the pathogenesis of SMS. 
GAD is the key enzyme in the synthesis of GABA, 
the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain. 
GAD has also been found in pancreatic p-cells and at 
lower levels, in the ludneys, liver, adrenal glands, 
ovary, and testes [lS). Two closely related GAD iso- 
forms (with molecular masses of 59 and 67 kd) have 
been identified in the brain and in the pancreas. The 
two isoforms are encoded by two different genes, have 
different intracellular distributions, and show different 
functional properties rib- 191. While the role of 
GABA in the brain has been established, little is 
known about the role of GAD and GABA in other 
tissues. 
GAD was recently identified as the 64-kd autoanti- 
gen recognized by sera from IDDM patients [20, 21) 
and is also a major target of islet-cell autoantibodies 
171, a highly predictive marker of IDDM 122). Sera 
positive for islet-cell autoantibodies are classified ac- 
cording to the selectivity of their islet-cell staining 
[23]: A first subgroup carries GAD-specific, p-cell- 
restricted islet-cell autoantibodies, while a second sub- 
group shows reactivity against antigens, other than 
GAD, present in all endocrine cells within pancreatic 
islets. Although only the latter subtype of islet-cell au- 
toantibodies is predictive of IDDM, an overall concor-

patients, reflects a common pathogenetically meaning-

We found evidence of autoimmune activation in 
two-thirds of patients with SMS. Support to a specific 
GAD autoantibody-mediated pathogenesis was ob- 
tained only in half of these patients (usually female 
patients with a diffuse polyendocrine autoreactivity). 
In the remaining half, the latter mechanism could not 
be advocated: Serum samples from the 4 SMS patients 
with an associated neoplasm, for example, did not show 
anti-GAD antibodies. Instead, they strongly recog- 
nized a brain protein of 1251130 kd. It is tempting to 
speculate that these patients represent a paraneoplastic 
subgroup. This 1251130-kd protein, as seen in other 
paraneoplastic autoimmune syndromes [26f, could be 
a constitutive component of neuronal cells able to trig- 
ger a strong autoimmune reaction. Characterization of 
this protein might lead to a better understanding of the 
pathogenesis underlying some cases of SMS. 
We also identified another subgroup of SMS patients 
(mainly male) without polyendocrine autoreactivity or 
evidence of anti-GAD antibodies. In the absence of 
any other clue on the nature of these patients’ illness, 
we presently consider them as affected by idiopathic 
SMS. 
If anti-GAD autoantibodies are not necessarily asso- 
ciated with SMS, how do we then explain their appear- 
ance in some but not all SMS patients? These auto- 
antibodies may represent a mere epiphenomenon 
unrelated, at least in the majority of SMS patients, to 
the pathogenesis of the disease. A pathological process 
against central nervous system structures rich in GAD 
might release normally sequestered molecules, which 
might become targets for an autoimmune response. 
Alternatively, autosensitization against GAD may actu- 
ally arise at the level of pancreatic @-cells and cross- 
react with central nervous system cells rich in GAD. 
This mechanism, although potentially able to cause 
pathological changes in all exposed individuals, does so 
in only a subgroup of SMS patients with other predis- 
posing factor(s); in fact, sporadic juvenile [27) cases of 
SMS or with autosomal dominant genetic [28], infec- 
tious (291, or paraneoplastic {7-11, 303 origin have 
been described. 
In conclusion, our study indicates that SMS is a het- 
erogeneous disorder and can be subdivided into three 
main subgroups: (1) SMS patients (mostly female) who 
have associated autoimmune diseases (mainly IDDM) 
and who test positive for islet-cell autoantibodies, anti- 
GAD antibodies, and organ-specific autoantibodies, 
and negative for non-organ-specific autoantibodies 
(autoimmune SMS); (2) SMS patients (mostly male) 
who have associated neoplasms and frequently have 
non-organ-specific autoantibodies, but who test nega- 
tive for islet-cell autoantibodies, anti-GAD antibodies, 
or organ-specific autoantibodies (paraneoplastic SMS); 
and (3) SMS patients who have no other associated 
clinical conditions but who show a high prevalence of 
non-organ-specific autoantibodies, but no islet-cell au- 
toantibodies, anti-GAD antibodies, or organ-specific 
autoantibodies (idiopathic SMS). In the paraneoplastic 
subgroup of SMS patients, we frequently detected an 
antibody directed against an unknown 125/ 130-kd

protein, suggesting that central nervous system anti- 
gens other than GAD may be the target of autoimmu- 
nity in SMS patients. 
Our findings indicate that the diagnosis of SMS 
should remain clinical and that the absence of circulat- 
ing anti-GAD antibodies does not exclude a diagnosis 
of SMS. Other central nervous system molecules can 
be the target of an autoimmune attack in some patients 
with SMS. The pathogenetic relevance of these autoan- 
tibodies, as well as that of anti-GAD antibodies, de- 
serves further scrutiny. Moreover, clinical evidence of 
continuous motor-unit hyperactivity should alert the 
clinician to the possible existence of an associated neo- 
plasm. 
Addendum 
After this article was accepted for publication, a study 
was published reporting on 3 patients with SMS, circu-

328:546-55 1). Thus, the total number of patients 
with paraneoplastic SMS associated with antibodies 
to a 125-130 kd protein reported so far is 5 (one 
patient was included in both studies).

Genetics of susceptibility and resistance to
insulin-dependent diabetes in stiff-man
syndrome
SiR-Stiff-man syndrome (SMS) is a rare disorder of the
central nervous system characterised by muscle rigidity and
spasms. Autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) are found in 60% of patients,’ suggesting an
autoimmune pathogenesis. SMS is often associated with
other autoimmune diseases including insulin-dependent
diabetes mellitus (IDDM). Since GAD is an autoantigen
both in SMS and IDDM, the two diseases may correlate
with different immune responses to GAD that are at least in
part genetically determined.
We have HLA typed 18 SMS patients’ and found that, as
in IDDM, SMS was associated with the allele DQB1*0201.

Other DQB1 alleles rarely found in IDDM (*0602 and
sequence-related *06 alleles) were found in 10 SMS patients
at the frequency observed in controls. 5 of 8 SMS patients
lacking a *06 allele had diabetes by contrast with 2 of 10
patients with a *06 allele, suggesting that *06 might be
associated with a reduced prevalence of diabetes in SMS. To
test this hypothesis we followed up our SMS patients for the
possible development of diabetes.
Since our 1993 report3 additional SMS patients now have
diabetes. All 3 patients had DQB1*0201 and 2 lacked *06
alleles. Diabetes has thus now developed in 7 of 8 SMS
patients lacking a *06 allele and in 3 of 10 with a *06 allele
(p=002). 10 of 13 SMS patients with 1*0201 have diabetes
versus 3 of 10 of those with a *06 allele (p=003).

relatives of IDDM patients with *0602 and SMS-like GAD
autoantibodies are at very low risk of diabetes.4 Perhaps an
SMS-like-anti-GAD response is associated with different
rates of progression to overt diabetes depending on the HLA
genetic background. Diabetes may develop very slowly or
not at all in individuals with a subset of anti-GAD
autoantibodies and IDDM-protective DQB1 alleles. We
suggest that DQB1*0602 (and other sequence-related *06
alleles) confers protection from diabetes in patients with

autoantibodies. By contrast, among SMS patients, 1*0201 is
associated with high risk of diabetes, especially when

as well as reflex-like induced violent spasms were the 
prominent features. Stiffness was the initial symptom of

violent whole-body jerks with a brisk onset and a succes-

Article abstract-We performed a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of intrathecal baclofen (ITB) in stiff-man syndrome. Three patients, unresponsive to current therapy, received 50 pg of ITB or placebo on sequential days. Following
ITB, all patients demonstrated improvement in reflex EMG activity. The mean reduction in total EMG activity (from

the others studied by a longer duration of disease, greater severity of stiffness, less fear of falling, and greater electrophysiologic improvement.

Discussion. Despite our small sample size, we were
able t o detect a significant electrophysiologic response in SMS following ITB as evidenced by the reduction in total reflex EMG activity and prolongation
of the onset latency of the cutaneous flexor reflex.
The cutaneous flexor reflex is one of several exteroceptive reflexes consistently exaggerated in
SMS.12J3J5Presumably, these reflex abnormalities
reflect hyperexcitability along polysynaptic reflex
arcs, most prominently at the spinal level. We observed maximal reflex EMG activity following medial plantar nerve stimulation, and found that this
reflex could be reliably measured without habituation during the testing protocol, making it an excellent physiologic measure of SMS. Other electrophysiologic techniques are of limited value in evaluating the effects of treatments in SMS. Monosynaptic reflex arcs are usually normal,12 and although documentation of continuous muscle activOctober 1995 NEUROLOGY 45 1895

ity is useful in the initial evaluation of SMS, it may
be absent in rested patients on medical therapy.
This was apparent to us during the pretrial evaluation of our patients, and for this reason we did not
employ this technique during the trial.
Two aspects of the electrophysiologic response in
our patients bear further comment. The reflex
EMG activity was most markedly suppressed in
the legs and paraspinal muscles, consistent with
the known gradient of distribution of ITB following
lumbar intrathecal administration.EThis pattern of
response may also, i n part, reflect the known
greater hyperexcitability of t r u n k a n d lowerextremity muscles in SMS.15 The prolongation of
t h e onset latency i n t h e proximal leg a n d
paraspinal muscles cannot be explained with certainty, but most likely reflects reduced temporal
summation along the flexor reflex pathways due to
baclofen’s effects on presynaptic inhibition and
postsynaptic neuronal excitability.16J7 Together,
these findings suggest that ITB was acting in a
local and inhibitory manner at the spinal level.
Although muscle stiffness was reduced in all patients, we were unable to document a statistically
significant change. This may be due to a combination of the small sample size and lack of sensitivity
of the Ashworth scale. Although we observed an
electrophysiologic response to ITB in all patients,
only one responded with clear clinical improvement. This patient was more severely affected, had
asymmetric involvement of the lower extremities,
had a longer duration of disease, and also showed
greater electrophysiologic improvement following
ITB. An insufficient dose, or a n early peak CSF
level of ITB, may account for the lesser electrophysiologic improvement in the two patients who
did not respond, but both patients reported increased unsteadiness of their legs and more difficulty walking following ITB, despite a reduction in
muscle stiffness. We interpret these changes as
treatment effects, and, together with the patients’
“fear of falling,” we felt that, following unblinding
of the first stage of the trial, a higher dose of ITB
would not benefit these patients. In these patients
(and in future trials), further evaluation of the effects of ITB would best be performed using continuous intrathecal infusion through an intraspinal
catheter to allow time for adaptation and to adjust
the dose if necessary.
Brashear and Phillips13 previously noted the discrepancy between the electrophysiologic and clinical responses. Their patient’s subjective clinical response was significantly delayed in comparison
with the observed changes in reflex muscle activity
and muscle stiffness. This further supports our
suggestion that a period of time may be needed in
these patients to allow for adaptation to changes in
their muscle tone, and that the exteroceptive reflexes are a sensitive indicator of changes in reflex
pathways important in the pathophysiology of
SMS.
In previously reported patients receiving ITB for

SMS, three showed an impressive response to longterm ITB.gJOPenn and Mangierig documented a response to an open test dose of 75 pg, although the
patient with advanced SMS, treated with a relatively limited dose of ITB (120 pg/d), showed longterm improvement in spasms and pain, but no
functional improvement because of lower-extremity
ankylosis. Ford and Fahnll reported a similar patient with advanced SMS, a relatively fixed increased lumbar lordosis, and ankylosis of the hips,
who showed no improvement following doubleblind administration of bolus test doses up to 100
bg. The pattern of response in these patients, together with t h e SMS patients reported in our
study, suggests that those most likely to benefit
from ITB are those with moderately severe disease,
but without a fixed deformity or ankylosis. Of the
three patients reported in our trial, patient 3 has
recently commenced continuous long-term ITB infusion and is responding well to his current dose of
730 pg/day. The other two patients have currently
elected to continue their prestudy drug therapy,
but may undergo further evaluation in the future
using continuous infusion of ITB through an intraspinal catheter.
In summary, our trial has demonstrated a significant electrophysiologic improvement in SMS following ITB. Although this supports the suggested
efficacy of ITB in SMS,gJothe overall response in
our patients did not always parallel the electrophysiologic improvement. Long-term clinical efficacy remains to be proven, but we believe that ITB may be
efficacious in reducing the stiffness and spasms in
some patients with SMS. Continuous infusion may
be preferable to bolus administration for assessing
the response to ITB in selected patients.

Article abstract-The natural history and the clinical and neuroimaging features of brainstem tumors in neurofibromatosis type 1(NF1) are poorly understood. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been useful in NF1 in detecting intracranial abnormalities, especially of the brainstem. Brainstem tumors in NF1 have been confused clinically with
non-NF1 brainstem tumors and radiographically with the increased T, signal abnormalities, also known as “unidentified bright objects” (UBOs), which are common in NF1 and often located in the brainstem. This study, which evaluated
17 NF1 patients with brainstem tumors, is the largest series to date. Fifteen of 17 patients (88%)had neurologic signs
and symptoms referable to brainstem dysfunction, including dysarthria, cranial neuropathies, and gross motor incoordination. Tumors were located primarily in the medulla in 14 of 17 NF1 patients (82%), in contrast to the pontine
tumor location in the non-NF1 population. Seven NF1 patients (41%) required shunt placement for hydrocephalus at
initial diagnosis, more frequent than in non-NF1 brainstem tumor patients. Six of 17 patients (35%)had evidence of
radiographic tumor progression, but only three of them (18%) had correlative clinical progression. Two patients with
progressive symptoms had partial surgical resection, and pathology revealed either fibrillary or anaplastic astrocytomas. Three patients were treated with radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or both, with two deaths. With a median
follow-up of 52 months, 15 of 17 patients remain alive; 14 of them did not require adjuvant therapy. In our series, we
describe NF1 brainstem tumors as a distinct clinical entity, much less aggressive than non-NF1 pontine tumors but
more symptomatic than brainstem UBOs in NF1.

Using an immunoprecipitation assay to measure anti-GAD speci- 
ficity, our results demonstrate that the humoral response to GAD in 
SMS  is quite complex as reflected by the presence of several GAD 
autoantibody species directed at several regions of the GAD pro- 
tein. SMS and IDDM  sera differ in titer and epitope specificity of 
GAD Abs All SMS sera tested contained Abs to GAD 65 and 
GAD 67 at titers greater than 1/1000 in distinction to IDDM sera 
whose GAD autoantibodies bind GAD 65 only and can rarely be 
detected at  a greater titer than 1/100. In this fashion, individuals 
with SMS resemble individuals with the restricted ICA pattern 
(GAD-absorbable pattern) that has been associated with a low rate 
of progression to IDDM (23). SMS  sera also have Abs that bind 
GAD protein fragments consisting of the amino-, middle-, and 
carboxyl third of the GAD 65 protein. In contrast, the autoanti- 
bodies in IDDM sera react predominantly with GAD 65, do not 
bind GAD protein fragments or with denatured GAD protein by 
immunoblotting, and thus target GAD protein epitopes dependent 
on protein conformation (10, 23).
